questions.q: Why is a raw daily alert count, on its own, not very useful?
options: Raw alert counts are always the same number every single day
It doesn't show the breakdown by severity and source that actually points to a tuning candidate
SIEMs are incapable of reporting a raw alert count accurately
Alert counts can only be measured once a year
questions.explain: A useful version breaks the total down by shift, severity, and source — that's what turns a raw number into something actionable.

questions.q: What do analyst workload metrics like "alerts per analyst per shift" and "time per alert" actually measure?
options: The number of correlation rules currently active
How many systems are connected to the SIEM as log sources
What handling the incoming alert volume actually costs the humans doing the triage
The total number of alerts a SIEM can process per second
questions.explain: Workload metrics describe the human side of alert volume — how much work each analyst is actually carrying.

questions.q: A SOC sees alerts-per-analyst rise from 50 to 80 while average time per alert drops from 6 minutes to under 3. What does this combination most likely indicate?
options: Analysts are under-resourced for the volume and rushing triage, not that the work got easier
Nothing meaningful — these two numbers are unrelated to each other
The SIEM's correlation rules have become more accurate
Alert volume has decreased significantly
questions.explain: Read together, a rising per-analyst load with a shrinking time-per-alert points to analysts moving faster than careful triage allows, usually because staffing hasn't kept pace.

questions.q: What does a growing backlog of alerts carried over from one shift to the next typically signal?
options: That all alerts from that shift were false positives
That the SIEM has stopped generating new alerts
That the dashboard needs more vanity metrics added
That staffing on that shift hasn't matched the incoming alert volume
questions.explain: A backlog that keeps growing shift over shift is a workload signal pointing directly at a staffing gap.

questions.q: What is "alert fatigue," and why is it a genuine detection risk rather than just a morale issue?
options: A term for alerts that are automatically closed by the SIEM after 24 hours
The risk that analysts under sustained high alert volume start dismissing alerts too quickly to keep pace, which can let a real attack through
A medical condition unrelated to SOC staffing or workload
The natural decrease in alert volume that happens over a weekend
questions.explain: Analysts sustained at a high alerts-per-shift rate for weeks are more likely to rubber-stamp alerts as false positives just to keep the queue moving, which can let a real incident slip through.
